paper.title: MobileInject: Evaluating Reasoning-to-Action Security of MLLM-Based Mobile Agents under Cross-Modal Consistency Injection
paper.central_claim: MobileInject systematically measures mobile-agent security with 108 executable instances across 11 scenarios and nine risk categories; cross-modal consistent injection and MRCD/RCI expose reasoning-to-action vulnerabilities, RSDF diagnoses their propagation, and existing prompt defenses are insufficient.

evidence.quote:
### 3.1 Design Principles and Threat Model

Design Principles. MobileInject is guided by four principles. First, ecological realism : attacks are embedded in executable, interactive, and stateful mobile workflows, thereby preserving cross-app interactions, dynamic interface changes, and action consequences. Second, systematic coverage : the benchmark encompasses diverse scenarios, workflows, injection vectors, attack goals, and security outcomes. Third, controllable and extensible attack design : injections are defined as configurable templates that can be composed along dimensions such as modality, vector, and complexity. Fourth, trajectory-level observability : MobileInject records step-by-step observations, reasoning, actions, goals, and states, thereby enabling fine-grained diagnosis beyond binary safe/unsafe labels.

Threat Model. MobileInject adopts a trusted-instruction, untrusted-observation threat model. System instructions and explicit user task objectives define the trusted root, while all environmental observations during task execution are considered potentially untrusted. These observations include visual inputs (e.g., screenshots, images, webpages, emails, messages, social-media content, calendar events, and notifications) and textual inputs (e.g., XML hierarchies, accessibility trees, UI layouts, element attributes, application names, and other UI metadata).
Attacker can inject malicious payloads only through these observable surfaces, but cannot alter the system prompt, model parameters, operating system, or genuine user instructions. Payloads may appear in visual channel, textual channel, or both, forming cross-modal injections. This formulation treats cross-application content uniformly as part of the observation space and enables evaluation of realistic indirect attacks, including both unimodal and multimodal injections.

### 3.2 Benchmark Construction

Figure 3: Task distribution of MobileInject across human activity domains, application scenarios, malicious consequence categories, and benign task carriers.

High-Fidelity Environment. MobileInject executes each instance in a resettable Android emulator rather than as a static prompt–response sample. The agent observes the rendered screen and UI/XML structure, reasons over them, and interacts through taps, long presses, swipes, and text entry. Application and device states evolve after each action.

Benchmark Contents. MobileInject consists of a workflow-grounded core and a systematic payload stress layer. The core includes nine benign workflows—messaging, contact creation, email, social posting, note writing, file management, calendar, paper trading, and message-to-web navigation—covering 11 application scenarios. A workflow is included only if it satisfies five criteria: a common or safety-relevant user goal, a natural third-party-content carrier, feasible benign and malicious execution paths, a resettable initial state, and an objective state oracle. The stress layer defines 12 registered adversarial objectives spanning nine consequence categories: content misuse, privacy exposure, financial misconduct, privilege abuse, data-integrity compromise, resource abuse, hazardous-content access, discrimination, and phishing/social engineering. In total, MobileInject comprises 108 executable instances with persistent and realistically evolving states, each grounded in a concrete mobile workflow and equipped with resettable initialization and verifiable outcome oracles. Fig. 3 summarizes the coverage.

Six-Stage Construction. As shown in Fig. 2 , construction follows six stages: Goal Selection → \rightarrow State Initialization → \rightarrow Injection → \rightarrow Agent Execution → \rightarrow Dual Oracle → \rightarrow Trajectory Diagnosis . Concretely, we (1) select a registered benign–adversarial pair; (2) restore the corresponding Android snapshot and prepare the task-specific preconditions; (3) instantiate the adversarial GoalID in the designated screenshot and/or UI/XML carrier; (4) execute up to 20 agent actions while logging each observation, rationale, parsed action, target, and state transition; (5) evaluate benign and adversarial state predicates after each step; and (6) apply RSDF to the recorded trajectory for in-depth diagnosis of reasoning-to-action security. This benchmark evaluates the reasoning-to-action security of mobile agents under cross-modal injection pressure.

Table 2: MobileInject construction contract.

Component | Registered content
Scope | 11 scenarios; Visual and Textual Observations
Objectives | Registered benign workflows and adversarial payloads
Instance | snapshot, apps, carrier, workflow, two oracles
Execution | reset → \rightarrow inject → \rightarrow closed-loop agent actions
Evidence | observation, recorded rationale, action, UI/state, endpoints
Quality control | schema checks, oracle replay, carrier-contract checks

Instance Contract and Quality Control. Each record specifies its instance ID, apps, snapshot/reset procedure, initial state, carrier-specific payloads, expected workflow, step budget and seed, benign/adversarial oracles, and execution trace. Admission requires schema completeness, successful reset, payload visibility in the declared channel, executable benign and adversarial paths, and replayable oracle checks. Because the 108 instances reuse workflow and objective structures, they are not semantically or statistically independent; our analysis accounts for both dependencies.
evidence.support_explanation: Trust boundary, instance admission, reset and oracle protocol.

### 3.3 Cross-Modal Consistency Injection

The tested agents jointly receive a Visual Observation and a Textual Observation. CMCI varies where the same adversarial instruction is exposed: the visual channel only, the textual channel only, or both. In the dual-channel condition, identical injected content appears in rendered application content (e.g., a message, email, webpage, or post) and in the corresponding textual interface representation. Equal-exposure controls then isolate the Cross-Modal Reinforcement Effect from repeated presentation.

We retain the original task-level formulation. For episode i i at step t t , let O i , t v O^{v}_{i,t} and O i , t x O^{x}_{i,t} denote the Visual and Textual Observations.  | I i b \displaystyle I_{i}^{b} | = φ ( b i ) , I i a = ϕ ( g i ) . \displaystyle=\varphi(b_{i}),\quad I_{i}^{a}=\phi(g_{i}). | 

Here, φ \varphi and ϕ \phi are the registered benign- and adversarial-instruction templates. The modality constructors C v C_{v} and C x C_{x} place I i a I_{i}^{a} in their channel-specific carriers; they are distinct from the completion contracts C i b , C i a C_{i}^{b},C_{i}^{a} . CMCI then constructs the poisoned observation

 | O ~ i , t = ( O i , t v ⊕ C v ​ ( I i a ) , O i , t x ⊕ C x ​ ( I i a ) ) , \widetilde{O}_{i,t}=\bigl(O^{v}_{i,t}\oplus C_{v}(I_{i}^{a}),\;O^{x}_{i,t}\oplus C_{x}(I_{i}^{a})\bigr), |  | (2)

where ⊕ \oplus denotes the injection operation. Cross-modal consistency directly requires the two carriers to contain the same adversarial instruction:

 | Content ⁡ ( C v ​ ( I i a ) ) = Content ⁡ ( C x ​ ( I i a ) ) = I i a . \operatorname{Content}\!\left(C_{v}(I_{i}^{a})\right)=\operatorname{Content}\!\left(C_{x}(I_{i}^{a})\right)=I_{i}^{a}. |  | (3)

Thus, “consistent” means exactly that the visual and textual injections present the same adversarial instruction, as defined in Eq. 3 .

The original ablation shows that aligned cross-modal injections achieve lower utility and higher attack success than either text-only or visual-only injections (Section 5 ). To disentangle this gain from repeated exposure, we compare five conditions in Fig. 11 : TOI and VOI present the injected instruction once through the textual or visual channel; TOI+ and VOI+ repeat it twice within the same channel; and CMCI presents it once in each channel. CMCI retains a clear endpoint advantage over both equal-exposure same-channel controls. The controlled ordering rules out duplicate exposure as a sufficient explanation, and the matched trajectories then localize the cross-modal goal-switch pathway.

Matched trajectories explain why cross-modal injection succeeds when either single-channel condition fails. Among the 108 paired instances, 30 exhibit the same reversal pattern: neither VOI nor TOI reaches the adversarial state, whereas aligned CMCI does. In these cases, the visual occurrence grounds the injected instruction in the current interface, while its textual UI/XML occurrence makes the same instruction directly interpretable and actionable. Their alignment induces a priority shift from the trusted user goal to the injected objective, which then propagates into unsafe actions. The equal-exposure controls show that it cannot be explained by repeated presentation alone.

### 3.4 Reinforced Injection Methods

For Q.2, MobileInject introduces two complementary template families under a fixed adversarial objective: MRCD supplies role-like authority, priority, and consent cues, while RCI supplies externally visible pseudo-rationale shaped to the current task context. The ablations and matched controls verify their complementary contributions.

Multi-Role Collaborative Deception. This method constructs multiple role-like external signals to jointly support the same adversarial objective. Unlike presenting a single malicious instruction, the injected content frames the objective as a high-priority, apparently user-initiated, consent-confirmed, urgent, and rationalized task. Specifically, this method simulates role fragments that correspond to authority-like priority, user goal declaration, consent confirmation, and action rationale, respectively. These fragments do not truly grant system authority or represent user consent; instead, they test whether the agent incorrectly treats role-like text in the environment as trusted control information. This method therefore stresses whether the agent can preserve the boundary between trusted instructions and untrusted observations when environmental content imitates authority, consent, and task justification.

Reasoning-Camouflage Injection. RCI exposes the adversarial objective through three visible components: current app context, a bridge from the benign task state, and the registered adversarial instruction. Rather than creating an abrupt goal discontinuity, it frames the malicious request as the locally coherent next step of the ongoing task. The context anchors the injection to the current observation, and the bridge justifies replacing the benign next action. The agent may then internalize this pseudo-rationale and propagate the goal switch into its action plan. Fig. 4 illustrates the mechanism. Section 5 shows through ablations that RCI consistently improves endpoint attack success across all six base attacks; matched controls further rule out length, repetition, exposure rounds, and interface salience as sufficient explanations.

Section 5 reports gains for MRCD and RCI together with budget-matched reinforced baselines. The full setting remains stronger after matching template length, repetition, exposure rounds, and interface salience, excluding those factors as sufficient explanations for its endpoint advantage.
evidence.support_explanation: Single-channel, consistent two-channel and matched-exposure interventions; MRCD/RCI operation.

## 4 Reasoning Security Diagnosis Framework

RSDF complements state-verified endpoints with evidence-grounded diagnosis of the externally recorded execution trace. As summarized in Fig. 2 , it contains five modules with distinct responsibilities: (1) Trajectory Collector records the post-exposure observation, emitted rationale, executed action and target, and resulting device state; (2) State Verifier evaluates benign and adversarial completion using deterministic Android/application oracles; (3) Reasoning Diagnoser assigns evidence-localized awareness, rationale-hijack, and action-hijack labels; (4) Profile Aggregator converts finalized labels and oracle outcomes into episode- and model-level metrics; and (5) Visual Reporter presents the metric profile together with representative evidence-bearing trajectories. This separation prevents semantic diagnosis from replacing state verification.

For every step after first payload exposure, the Trajectory Collector stores

 | τ i = { ξ i , t } t = 1 L i , ξ i , t = ( O ~ i , t , r i , t , a i , t , e i , t , s i , t ) , \tau_{i}=\{\xi_{i,t}\}_{t=1}^{L_{i}},\qquad\xi_{i,t}=(\widetilde{O}_{i,t},r_{i,t},a_{i,t},e_{i,t},s_{i,t}), |  | (4)

where r i , t r_{i,t} , a i , t a_{i,t} , e i , t e_{i,t} , and s i , t s_{i,t} denote the model-emitted rationale, executed action, action target, and resulting device state. This record preserves the evidence needed to distinguish a stated intention from an executed, state-changing action.

Two deterministic state oracles map the trajectory and the instance contracts to the observed endpoint pair:

 | ( y i b , y i a ) = 𝒱 ⁡ ( τ i , C i b , C i a ) , y i b , y i a ∈ { 0 , 1 } . (y_{i}^{b},y_{i}^{a})=\mathcal{V}(\tau_{i};C_{i}^{b},C_{i}^{a}),\qquad y_{i}^{b},y_{i}^{a}\in\{0,1\}. |  | (5)

Here, y i b y_{i}^{b} and y i a y_{i}^{a} report benign and adversarial completion, respectively. They are verified against Android/application state rather than inferred from the tested agent’s response.

Let E i = { t i exp , … , L i } E_{i}=\{t_{i}^{\mathrm{exp}},\ldots,L_{i}\} be the post-exposure window. For each t ∈ E i t\in E_{i} , an automated semantic evaluator separate from the tested mobile agent proposes the diagnostic vector. Deterministic trace anchors, endpoint-consistency anchors, and a conflict checker then accept, modify, or route it to automated conflict-directed adjudication:

 | 𝐳 i , t \displaystyle\mathbf{z}_{i,t} | = 𝒜 ⁡ ( ξ i , t , Γ ) = ( z i , t aw , z i , t rh , z i , t ah ) , \displaystyle=\mathcal{A}(\xi_{i,t};\Gamma)=(z_{i,t}^{\mathrm{aw}},z_{i,t}^{\mathrm{rh}},z_{i,t}^{\mathrm{ah}}), |  | (6)
 | ρ i , t \displaystyle\rho_{i,t} | = μ ⁡ ( z i , t rh , z i , t ah ) ∈ { SA , AD , RCO , FH } . \displaystyle=\mu(z_{i,t}^{\mathrm{rh}},z_{i,t}^{\mathrm{ah}})\in\{\mathrm{SA},\mathrm{AD},\mathrm{RCO},\mathrm{FH}\}. | 

The three labels denote injection-specific awareness, recorded-rationale hijack, and action hijack. Awareness requires an explicit link to the injected source, conflict, or risk; generic caution is insufficient. Rationale hijack requires adoption or material advancement of g i g_{i} , rather than quotation alone. Action hijack requires an executed or pending action that substantively advances the adversarial oracle. The implemented pipeline additionally enforces that an episode whose adversarial state oracle fires contains at least one action-hijack label and, when rationale is available, at least one rationale-hijack label; the merger can assign a fallback positive step and applies outcome-dependent rationale persistence. These outcome-constrained diagnostics align the semantic labels with verified execution, while their evidence spans localize the transition from malicious-goal adoption to unsafe action.
evidence.support_explanation: Independent endpoint verification but outcome-constrained semantic diagnosis, including forced fallback positives and persistence.

evidence.quote:
Evaluated MLLMs and Agent Frameworks. We conduct a large-scale evaluation on MobileInject to assess the fine-grained reasoning-to-action security of 2 × 9 2\times 9 MLLM-based mobile agents in realistic mobile workflows. Specifically, we pair two agent frameworks, M3A Agent [ 19 ] and MobAgent [ 11 ] , with nine representative open- and closed-source MLLMs: GLM-4.5V [ 9 ] , GLM-4.6V [ 36 ] , Qwen2.5-VL-72B [ 16 ] , Qwen3.5-122B [ 17 ] , Qwen3.6-35B-A3B [ 18 ] , Gemini-2.5-Flash/Gemini-3-Flash [ 7 ] , GPT-4.1 [ 13 ] , and GPT-5.4-Nano [ 14 ] .

Supported Attack and Defense Methods. MobileInject covers a diverse set of attack and defense methods. On the attack side, Direct , Ignore , InjecAgent , Important , and Manipulation respectively cover direct indirect instructions, rule-overriding prompt injection, benchmark-style intensified injection, high-priority message framing, and multi-turn attack methods [ 37 , 5 , 11 ] . On the defense side, Data Delimiters , Prescriptive , SCoT , Safe Guide , and Safety Sandwich respectively cover input separation, rule-based safety prompting, structured safety reasoning, general safety guidance, and sandwiching strategies [ 35 , 5 , 21 , 11 ] . Length, objective repetition, exposure rounds, and interface salience are explicit covariates in the matched MRCD/RCI protocol.

Evaluation Metrics. Following agent safety benchmarks that jointly consider benign utility and adversarial success [ 37 , 5 , 11 ] , we report both outcome-level and trajectory-level metrics. Outcome-level metrics include UC, UA, AGR, and OCM. RSDF further reports SAR, RHR, RHOR, RHD, AHR, AHAS, RATM, RACR, and the auxiliary OSS summary to diagnose risk perception, reasoning hijacking, action hijacking, and reasoning–action propagation.

Implementation Details. Experiments use a resettable Android emulator [ 19 , 11 ] . MobileInject contains 108 executable stateful instances, so every complete framework–model condition has N = 108 N=108 episodes. An episode begins from a task-specific snapshot and stops when the benign oracle fires, the adversarial oracle fires, the agent declares failure, or the step budget is exhausted. The two oracles are checked after every action. Most ablation and defense conditions presented in the original experimental table include the full set of 108 instances. For supported comparisons, we report cluster-paired inference; for the remaining conditions, we report point estimates over the full grid.
evidence.support_explanation: 108-instance conditions, common 20-action cap, stopping rules and scope of inference.

evidence.quote:
### 5.2 Ablation Study

Figure 11: Equal-exposure CMCI controls on Gemini-2.5-Flash, averaged over four major benign workflows. TOI/VOI denote one textual/visual exposure; TOI+/VOI+ denote two exposures within the same channel; CMCI uses one textual and one visual exposure and achieves the highest AGR.

Figure 12: Budget-matched attack controls on Gemini-2.5-Flash, averaged over four major benign workflows. The “+” baselines match the full CMCI setting with MRCD and RCI in length, objective repetitions, exposure rounds, and interface salience.

Ablation Study on CMCI. Fig. 7 first shows that aligned Visual–Textual injection produces the lowest UA and highest AGR. Fig. 11 then fixes the exposure count: repeating text changes AGR from 68.8% to 72.9%, and repeating the visual payload leaves AGR at 27.8%, whereas presenting the same content once in each channel reaches 85.4% AGR and 0.0% UA. This controlled result reveals the Cross-Modal Reinforcement Effect beyond repeated exposure. The 30/108 matched reversals further reveal its mechanism: visual grounding and textual executability jointly induce a priority switch that propagates into unsafe actions.

Ablation Study on MRCD. Fig. 8 shows that combining role-like cues strengthens MRCD. Fig. 12 then controls the principal alternatives: InjecAgent+, Manipulation+, and Important+ match the full reinforced setting in length, malicious-objective repetitions, exposure rounds, and interface salience. Their AGR ranges from 70.83% to 77.08%, whereas the full setting reaches 85.40% with 0.00% UA. Extra text and salience therefore do not fully explain the observed gain.

Ablation Study on RCI. Fig. 9 shows that adding RCI raises AGR by 5.6–16.7 percentage points across all six base attacks while reducing UA in every comparison. Together with the matched controls in Fig. 12 , this rules out length, repetition, exposure count, and salience as sufficient explanations for the full reinforced setting. The result supports the intended behavioral pathway: RCI makes the malicious request appear continuous with the current task, while MRCD supplies a high-priority role frame.
evidence.support_explanation: Four-workflow equal-exposure and matched-base controls; scoped CMCI and RCI improvements.

evidence.quote:
### 5.3 Additional Diagnostic Analysis

RATM Analysis. Fig. 10 uses the formally defined Safe Alignment (SA), Action Drift (AD), Reasoning Constraint (RCO), and Complete Hijack (FH) labels. FH accounts for a large fraction of observed post-exposure states for most models, while SA remains limited. By jointly labeling the emitted rationale and executed action at each step, RATM localizes how malicious-goal adoption propagates into the unsafe action path.

OCM Analysis. Table 6 decomposes the recorded episode endpoints by benign and adversarial oracle values. Safe-complete endpoints are rare for most models, whereas unsafe-fail endpoints are frequent. OCM complements the aggregate UA and AGR measures by showing which of the four endpoint combinations each model reaches.

Analysis of Risk Consequences. Table 7 reports objective-family results. These families map to 9 top-level risk consequences, including the merger of content tampering and data destruction under data-integrity compromise. Low UA and high AGR/RHR/AHR across several families demonstrate broad attack transfer and reasoning-to-action failures across distinct consequence categories.

Analysis across Different Normal Tasks. Table 8 shows failures across all implemented benign workflows, demonstrating that the observed vulnerabilities transfer across MobileInject’s diverse application and task contexts. MobileInject organizes its 108 executable instances around workflow-grounded mobile scenarios and systematic adversarial-payload coverage. Workflow realism comes from stateful tasks with natural untrusted-content carriers; the complete construction probes whether registered payloads transfer across workflow contexts.

### 5.4 Performance of Different Defense Methods under MobileInject

Table 9 shows that the evaluated prompt-level defenses provide only limited protection under MobileInject. Although SCoT raises OSS from 7.96 to 23.52 and lowers AGR from 83.33% to 70.37%, attack rates remain high; RHR and AHR still yield AGRs of 84.26% and 80.56%, and Safety Sandwich raises UA only to 9.26%. These results indicate that prompt-level guidance alone is insufficient to reliably preserve the trusted task under cross-modal injection pressure. More effective multimodal defenses are therefore needed, particularly mechanisms for source-aware observation filtering, cross-modal consistency checking, and state-grounded action verification. The archived B1–A10 pair illustrates this limitation. Without defense, the agent adopts the injected priority and executes the registered harmful query; with SCoT, it detects the risk at the first post-exposure decision and refuses, but the defended run also fails the benign oracle, revealing a clear safety–utility trade-off. Across the paired endpoint analysis, SCoT reduces AGR by 12.96 points, yet its cluster interval crosses zero ([ − - 3.70, 33.33]) and its Holm-adjusted value remains non-significant ( p Holm = 0.486 p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.486 ). Taken together, these results show that existing prompt-level defenses do not provide reliable protection under MobileInject and underscore the need for stronger multimodal safeguards for secure deployment of mobile agents.

### 5.5 RSDF and MobileInject Variance Analysis

Fig. 5 reports empirical repeated-run variances of at most 2.15 for the displayed RSDF metrics and 3.85 for the displayed endpoint metrics on the 0–100 scale, demonstrating stable measurements across the sampled reruns. For the three GLM-4.5V MobAgent endpoint matrices, the embedded seed field gives AGR values of 81.5% (2026; 88/108), 80.6% (2027; 87/108), and 83.3% (2028; 90/108), a 2.7-point range. The directory labels for the 2026 and 2028 files are swapped, so we use the embedded seed rather than the folder name. These endpoint matrices confirm within-condition repeatability; RSDF repeatability is reported from the archived diagnostic outputs shown in Fig. 5 .

evidence.quote:
Evolution of Personalized Agents. Personalized agents have evolved from language-only assistants into multimodal operators capable of planning, tool use, and interaction with stateful digital environments. Early methods such as ReAct coupled reasoning with external actions, showing that language models can support sequential decision-making beyond static response generation [ 34 ] . Tool-augmented and function-calling agents extended this paradigm by enabling API and application use for user goals [ 15 , 5 , 37 ] . Recent work has increasingly moved toward graphical and mobile interfaces: AppAgent, Mobile-Agent, and Mobile-Agent-v2 study smartphone interaction [ 38 , 25 , 24 ] ; OSWorld and AndroidWorld provide dynamic computer and Android environments [ 33 , 19 ] ; and DigiRL explores training device-control agents in the wild [ 1 ] . Collectively, these advances shift agents from prompt-centric assistants to operators over private, multimodal, and stateful environments, where untrusted external content may appear in both rendered and structured observations and directly influence actions. Security therefore depends not only on output harmlessness, but also on whether untrusted observations are treated as actionable instructions and whether their influence propagates from perception and reasoning to execution.

From Large-Model Security to Agent Security. Progress in multimodal understanding has been accompanied by growing attention to adversarial robustness and model security [ 28 , 29 , 26 , 31 , 32 , 27 , 30 ] . Large-model security initially focused on harmful generation, bias, privacy leakage, jailbreaks, and prompt robustness [ 40 , 23 ] . As models became integrated with tools, applications, and external data, risks shifted from text generation to observation consumption, tool invocation, state transitions, and multi-step execution. Indirect prompt injection exemplifies this shift: malicious instructions embedded in third-party content can be retrieved by an application or tool and induce attacker-preferred actions [ 8 , 35 , 37 ] . AgentDojo and ToolEmu evaluate tool-using or sandboxed agents [ 5 , 21 ] ; later studies expand evaluation to privacy leakage, financial loss, unsafe tool use, over-trust in tool outputs, and insufficient risk awareness [ 39 , 11 ] . In GUI and mobile settings, GhostEI-Bench and OS-Sentinel study environmental injection and trajectory-level safety detection [ 3 , 22 ] , while AgentDoG and DTAP emphasize realistic environments, red-teaming, and fine-grained risk attribution [ 12 , 4 ] .

Nevertheless, existing evaluations still lack a systematic benchmark for multimodal indirect injection in realistic mobile ecosystems. They neither test whether attacker-authored content in synchronized visual and textual views of the same mobile state reinforces the adversarial objective beyond either channel alone, nor diagnose when such observations redirect reasoning and whether that deviation propagates into unsafe actions and verified outcomes. Consequently, current evaluations cannot fully characterize the practical risk of multimodal injection or the security value of agents and defenses beyond aggregate success rates. These limitations motivate MobileInject, a high-fidelity benchmark for multimodal injection and fine-grained reasoning-security diagnosis in mobile agents.
evidence.support_explanation: Author-stated prior-art gap; not an independent full-text novelty audit.

evidence.quote: Multimodal large language model (MLLM)-based mobile agents are rapidly evolving from conversational assistants into autonomous systems that perceive, reason over, and act on smartphone environments. This capability also exposes a new security risk: adversaries can embed malicious objectives in cross-application mobile content and steer agent behavior through indirect multimodal injection. Although prompt injection has been studied in desktop and web settings, its cross-modal properties in mobile ecosystems remain poorly understood, and existing security analyses are still limited. To close this gap, we introduce MobileInject, the first benchmark for evaluating mobile agents against multimodal injection attacks and reasoning-to-action security risks. MobileInject provides a high-fidelity interactive mobile evaluation framework covering 11 scenarios, 9 security-risk categories, and 108 executable risk instances. It further introduces Cross-Modal Consistency Injection to exploit corroboration across modalities, two enhanced attack methods, Multi-Role Collaborative Deception and Reasoning-Camouflage Injection, to intensify trust manipulation and reasoning hijacking, and a Reasoning Security Diagnosis Framework for fine-grained failure analysis. Systematic experiments show that mobile agents are broadly vulnerable to multimodal injection, and that many failures stem from reasoning hijacking at early stages. These findings establish MobileInject as a systematic cross-modal benchmark for studying and improving the security of mobile agents.
